Wizard Works Zambini Rack Bag Review: The Art of Rummaging

Bikepacking Gear / Bikepacking Bags

By Miles Arbour

Associate Editor & Events Manager

2,596 Posts

The new Wizard Works Zambini Rack Bag features a roll-top closure, exterior pockets, a simple four-point attachment system, and a waterproof liner. Miles spent the past three months testing both a pre-production version and a finalized model ahead of today’s release to see how it stacks up against other rack-top bags. Find his review here after several overnighters and a spin on the Arizona Trail…

PUBLISHED Nov 24, 2026

Instaread

What bikes we ride, the bags we use, and the gear we cram into them are inherently personal, but they also change depending on the trip, conditions, terrain, and the other gear we’re using. The way I pack for a singletrack-heavy route, for example, differs greatly from a route that’s mostly gravel roads and non-technical terrain. To get more specific, I like a mix of bag styles: stuffable dry bags on a cradle or rack for bulky gear like sleeping bags and down jackets, and a top-opening handlebar bag or rack-top bag for quick-access items. It doesn’t always pan out this way, but using a hybrid of bag styles usually checks all the boxes for how I ride, pack, and access gear.

One of the latest puzzle pieces is the rack-top bag, a perfect middle ground when you don’t need the capacity of panniers but want more than a seat pack. Some might say rack-top bags have been around forever, starting as commuter-style trunk bags, and there’s no denying they have influenced modern takes. Still, the latest wave of bags is more durable, more minimal, more stable on rough terrain, and often fully waterproof without a rain cover. A dry bag lashed onto a rack is a great place to start, but additional functionality and features, when executed well, work excellently as part of a larger bag system.

Wizard Works in the UK has a proclivity for top-opening bags. Browsing their massive collection, you’ll often see top-opening roll-tops favored over other designs. According to Wizard Works, they think the ability to “rummage through one’s stuff is crucial to the art of adventuring.” Their waterproof, seam-taped liners, introduced last year, integrate nicely with this design. Knowing this, we figured it was only a matter of time before Wizard Works released a rack-top bag. That day has finally come.

From our sponsor; more content below...

Introducing the Zambini Rack Bag

Earlier this summer, Wizard Works co-owners Harry and Ve sent me a pre-production version of their latest release, the Zambini Rack Bag, to test and provide feedback before locking in the final design. I logged some serious mileage with the pre-production model, including a couple of local overnighters and a week on the Arizona Trail. The final version I received a few weeks ago is nearly identical to the first version but with a simplified closure. Otherwise, it’s the same bag.

The Zambini is a top-opening rack-top bag. It attaches to virtually any rear rack thanks to four straps that hitch around the top of the rack, then clip into matching buckles on the sides of the bag, pulling it down onto the rack. A middle compression strap loops around the rack platform and bag, providing additional stability and compression.

It’s constructed from your choice of exterior fabric, with durable Hypalon on the base and a floating high-viz orange liner inside. While the exterior fabrics aren’t fully waterproof due to the sewn construction, the liner is taped and fully waterproof, keeping your gear dry. The seam-taping is on the backside of the fabric, which protects it from the gear you stuff inside the bag. Plus, if there’s ever a problem, the liner can be repaired or replaced. The bag’s front has a slight slant, leaving more room for your seatpost or dropper post, and the large roll-top opening has plastic stiffeners just below the opening to keep it clean and tidy.

The pre-production version I tested had the option to clip the buckles on the roll-top closure inside the front and rear pockets, but that ended up being awkward to use, so the final version just clips together like any standard dry bag. The mesh pockets at either end have adjustable shock-cord openings, and a small internal sleeve pocket on the back adds organization. The entire bottom half of the Zambini maintains its shape thanks to an internal plastic structure. One side has a sewn-in, pass-through slot for the compression strap, and the other has a D-ring that makes it a little easier to feed the strap through during installation or removal.

Like most of Wizard Works’ bags, the Zambini is available in a variety of stock colors, and you can also order it as a custom bag with your choice of color/fabric combinations. The final version I tested features a bright pink UltraGrid upper and a black Ultra body that looks super slick. The pre-production version was made entirely of tan 500-denier Cordura.

From our sponsor; more content below...

The Art of Adventure

Wizard Works has something unique in the Zambini Rack Bag. Although most of the elements exist on other bags, its unique combination of features sets it apart. Compared to other top-opening rack bags I’ve used, the Zambini has proven to be more stable and less prone to movement. The bag’s structured sides, Hypalon base, four-point girth-hitch attachment, and central compression strap work together to create a voluminous yet rock-solid rack bag.

I’d consider the section of Arizona Trail I rode some of the roughest singletrack I’ve bikepacked, and I was constantly surprised at how solid the Zambini felt out back mounted to my Sklar Lightweight Rack. I had the same experience running it on the Mica Rat Tail rack, which Wizard Works now sells, before that. I wondered if it would be as stable on a rack with a flat top deck, like those from Old Man Mountain, because of its slightly rounded base, but its semi-flexible construction means it works well on just about any style of rear rack. That said, I found it worked best and left more room for saddle/dropper post clearance when it wasn’t crammed close to the seatpost, like some racks do.

A small but important detail is the girth hitch straps that Wizard Works made for the Zambini. While they might not look like much, the rubber straps that connect to the rack have a clever tapered shape that helps the girth hitch lock in place when you loop it around the rack. I’ve used bags that rely on hook-and-loop or webbing straps, but Wizard Works’ custom straps offer far more grip, which helps keep the bag in place on rough terrain. When you get to camp, you simply release the center compression strap, unclip the four girth-hitch straps, and the Zambini is free from the bike. The process is fast enough that it could also make a functional bag for commuting, when the capacity of panniers isn’t required. After you remove the bag, the opposing male and female buckles connect so you can still ride without the straps getting caught in the wheel, although the tail end of the webbing straps still rubs on the tire.

On both of my trips with the Zambini, I paired it with a front roll, which isn’t easy to access on the fly. The Zambini satisfied all my rummaging needs thanks to its massive top-opening design. Since the four main straps don’t interfere with the opening, it’s easy to unclip the compression strap and open the roll-top closure. On the Arizona Trail, I used the less stuffable top-opening design to hold my Hyperlite CrossPeak 2 Tent, various camp accessories, my rain jacket, and some food. I still don’t think top-opening bags like the Zambini are the most efficient choice for stuffing bulky gear like sleeping bags or puffy jackets, but they can work when paired with compression sacks or another, more stuffable bag elsewhere.

Although they’re not massive, the two exterior mesh pockets have proven to be surprisingly useful. With the drawstring shock-cord closure, they are secure enough to hold dense items like spare sealant and fuel canisters, but they also work well for holding ground sheets, trash, and waterproof overgloves. The pocket at the rear saw a bit of spray from my rear tire, which is reason enough to not stash anything wearable there.

I had a surprisingly wet week on the Arizona Trail, and the Zambini’s waterproof liner did an excellent job at keeping my gear dry. The only time it got wet was when I had to open it up to find my rain jacket, which is one drawback of top-opening bags in general, but I’d confidently ride in heavy rain knowing its contents would stay dry. I hardly used the small internal drop pocket since it gets lost among everything inside, but it could be a place to stash keys or a passport.

From our sponsor; more content below...

Specs & Comparisons

Harry at Wizard Works explained that the primary goal was to design a rack bag that was both quick to access and quick to remove while also fitting a wide range of racks. From what I’ve experienced, the Zambini Rack Bag delivers on these ambitions and more. Not only is it one of the most stable rack-top bags I’ve used, but the Zambini is also yet another example of Wizard Works’ obsession with good product design.

In the comparison chart below, the Zambini is easily the heaviest top-opening rack bag, edged out only by the Tailfin CargoPack and Restrap Switch Top Bag, both of which are rack-specific. Browsing our Rack-Top Bag Gear Index, the Zambini is also one of the most expensive of the bunch, but it feels a step above most other bags in how it executes its features.

Universal Top-Opening Rack Bags Compared

Product Weight Volume Waterproof? Price/set (USD)
Wizard Works Zambini 570g 12L Yes £175 (~$230 USD)
Dispersed Rack Bag 250g 10L Yes, with dry bag $130
Rogue Panda Picketpost 235g 12L Yes $150
7Roads PackTrain 305g 14L Yes €141 (~$150 USD)
Old Man Mountain Juniper Trunk 295g 7L Yes $125
Skyler of Mica Cycles with his mega-mullet Esker Japhy. The original Zambini clipped down to buckles inside the mesh pockets, but Wizard Works ditched this based on tester feedback.

The Zambini is available and ready to ship as part of Wizard Works’ Core Range, made from 1000-denier (splatter) or 500-denier (black, olive, tan) Cordura. You can also order it as a custom order in any fabric from Wizard Works’ extensive range. Going the custom route also gives the chance to lower the overall weight, since Ultra and X-Pac fabrics weigh less than Cordura. They can also improve abrasion resistance and waterproofing scores.

I’ve now tested the original tan pre-production model and a custom UltraGrid/Ultra 200TX version, and I prefer the latter for the slight weight decrease (~80 grams); I also found the UltraGrid main closure easier to roll than the Cordura version on the Core Range. In heavy rain, the Cordura exterior held onto water weight more than the custom alternatives, which can add a surprising amount. No matter what version you get, the Zambini functions more like a handlebar bag for your rack, holding its shape no matter how full it’s packed, which is one of the downsides of strapping a dry bag to a rack.

Nic’s Thoughts

Nic: I used a prototype of the Wizard Works Zambini for a few overnighters this year and was generally happy with the experience. The bag is spacious, offers plenty of room through the roll-top closure for awkward, space-consuming gear—like a sleeping bag—and is made with the quality we’ve come to expect from Wizard Works. Its attachment system is also rock solid and stays out of the way. The oblong shape is ideal for rack systems like the Mica Rat Tail and Tailfin Journey Rack, and it uses the space well. It’s another great addition to the category, especially since it’s waterproof. That said, I didn’t like a few design elements.

Something I didn’t love was the extra strap that runs across the middle of the bag. I understand its function, but it feels like an afterthought. I would much rather it be attached to the bag so it isn’t as easy to forget or lose. It may be user error, but I forgot to cinch it down once or twice, and it flew into my rear wheel.

Finally, I like that the small straps used to attach to the bag can stay mated to the rear rack, but they rub on the tire when not in use. The adjustment straps are long and hang low, and mine have been damaged by my rear tire over time. As a result, I’ve resorted to removing them when not in use, which takes away some of the convenience. Overall, it’s still a fantastic option for a rack-top bag. It’s intentionally made for the growing number of rear rack systems on the market, so it feels ideal for that use case.

From our sponsor; more content below...
  • Capacity: 12L
  • Material (as tested): Cordura, Hypalon / UltraGrid, Ultra, Hypalon
  • Weight: 570 grams (Core Range) / ~490 grams (Custom)
  • Place of Manufacture: London, UK
  • Price: Core: £175 / Custom: from £200
  • Manufacturer’s Details: Wizard Works

Pros

  • Stable and wobble-free, even on the roughest of trails.
  • Quick-release and quick-access top-opening design is best in its class.
  • Waterproof, thanks to a floating, seam-taped liner.
  • Roomy external mesh pockets are functional.
  • Option to customize fabrics and colors.
  • Holds shape and doesn’t lose stability when lightly packed.

Cons

  • Hitch strap tails can rub on rear tire, even when clipped together, on some narrow rack setups.
  • Heavy.
  • Pricey, but justifiably so for a high-quality, UK-made bag.
  • Cordura exterior can take on additional weight in heavy rain.

Wrap Up

There are many ways to spend time on a bike. You can pack minimally and focus on the riding itself, which is an incredibly rewarding, albeit bare-bones way to bikepack. On the other end of the spectrum, you can use the bike as a tool to travel but find the real joy in camping, visiting new places, and chatting with locals. While you can combine the two, I consider the Wizard Works Zambini Rack Bag best suited for trips with detours, lazy mornings, and lingering moments. If you’re purely focused on ditching excess weight, the Zambini might not be the ticket. However, if you appreciate the expandability of a top-opening bag and aren’t sold on panniers, it’s an exceptionally well-thought-out rack bag. I have a funny feeling Emily and I will be playing a lot of “rock-paper-scissors” in order to decide who gets to use the pink Zambini.
